Brief: Describe the Great Barrier Reef and the threats it faces. — about Ecology

1. The Great Barrier Reef supports an extraordinary diversity of life, including many vulnerable or endangered species, some of which may be endemic to the reef system.
2. Thirty species of cetaceans have been recorded in the Great Barrier Reef, including the dwarf minke whale, Indo-Pacific humpback dolphin, and the humpback whale.
3. Large populations of dugongs live there.
4. More than 1,500 fish species live on the reef, including the clownfish, red bass, red-throat emperor, and several species of snapper and coral trout.
5. Forty-nine species mass spawn, while eighty-four other species spawn elsewhere in their range.
6. Seventeen species of sea snake live on the Great Barrier Reef in warm waters up to 50 metres (160 ft) deep and are more common in the southern than in the northern section.
7. None found in the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area are endemic, nor are any endangered.
8. Six species of sea turtles come to the reef to breed: the green sea turtle, leatherback sea turtle, hawksbill turtle, loggerhead sea turtle, flatback turtle, and the olive ridley.
9. The green sea turtles on the Great Barrier Reef have two genetically distinct populations, one in the northern part of the reef and the other in the southern part.
10. Fifteen species of seagrass in beds attract the dugongs and turtles, and provide fish habitat.
11. The most common genera of seagrasses are Halophila and Halodule.
12. Saltwater crocodiles live in mangrove and salt marshes on the coast near the reef.
